extracted.intended_audience: BBC content makers, editors, presenters and producers (journalists and commissioning staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial guidelines on achieving 'due impartiality' across BBC output, covering definitions, when and how to include views, handling controversial subjects, duties for staff, use of technology, elections, series-based impartiality, and referrals to senior advisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality itself means not favouring one side over another. 'Due' means that the impartiality must be adequate and appropriate to the output, taking account of the subject and nature of the content, the likely audience expectation, and any signposting that may influence that expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due impartiality does not mean equal division of time to every view or that every facet must be represented on every occasion. Context, output genre and platform matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and diversity of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC must be inclusive, reflecting a breadth and diversity of opinion, across the output as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breadth may require political and cultural range and consideration of other variations (age, wealth, urban/rural, innovative/status quo). May require inclusion of opinions some groups find unpalatable or offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Content makers should seek to achieve 'due weight' rather than equal coverage: minority views or those less supported by evidence should not necessarily be given similar prominence or weight to those with more support or better evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due weight can be applied either within an item or across output as a whole; assess prominence relative to prevailing consensus and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission risks to impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be occasions when omission of views or other material could jeopardise impartiality or accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No view must be excluded as a matter of principle; content producers should make reasoned decisions and apply consistent editorial judgement about inclusion or omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to controversial subjects and current public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC applies due impartiality to all subjects, with particular requirements for 'political or industrial controversy and matters relating to current public policy', including where they occur outside news/current affairs (eg sport, drama, entertainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversial subjects can arise in health, education, world events, religion, science, culture, identity, ethics, and historical issues that become controversial again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether a subject is 'controversial'
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if subjects are controversial, consider: level of public and political contention; whether it's substantive in a nation/region/community; topicality; sensitivities of audience beliefs and cultures; whether the subject is serious; distinction between fact and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice is available from Editorial Policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range and prominence on controversial subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with 'controversial subjects', current public policy or political issues, ensure a wide range of significant views and perspectives are given due weight and prominence; opinion should be clearly distinguished from fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important when the controversy is active; see guidance on signposting and linked output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major matters require especially wide coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Major matters' (generally national/international importance or similar significance in a smaller area) require an appropriately wide range of significant views to be included and given due weight in each programme or web item or in clearly linked and timely programmes or items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Views and facts must not be misrepresented when dealing with major matters; extra care required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signposting when focusing on a single aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Output may explore a specific aspect of an issue and provide an opportunity for a single view, but this should be clearly signposted when dealing with controversial subjects or current public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge existence of a range of views and their weights; consider timeframe for reflecting other perspectives and whether they need inclusion in connected output; signpost links back and forward to related output explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: External links should represent a reasonable range
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a BBC online site covering 'controversial subjects' offers links to external sites, it should try to ensure that the information on those external sites, taken together, represents a reasonable range of views about the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See guidance on links and feeds and Section 15 on independence from external interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: News must be treated with due impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: News in whatever form must be treated with due impartiality, giving due weight to events, opinion and main strands of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach and tone must reflect BBC editorial values, including commitment to impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenters/journalists must not express personal opinions in news/current affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenters, reporters, correspondents and on-air editors must not enable audiences to tell their personal opinions on matters of current public policy, political or industrial controversy or other controversial subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may provide professional judgements rooted in evidence and experience, but may not express personal views publicly in BBC-branded output or on personal blogs/social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unintended bias and loaded language
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieving due impartiality requires awareness that unintended biases can result from loaded language, subconscious assumptions and choices about prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: phrases like 'the burden of taxation' may imply bias. Advice available from Editorial Policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expressions of opinion — personal responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals whose role requires impartiality must assess risk and take personal responsibility regarding what constitutes 'public' expression of opinion (including in closed groups or private meetings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should be cautious about expressions outside public broadcast and consider implications for perceived impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory referral for public expression or political candidacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual in a role requiring impartiality who intends to express opinions publicly on current public policy, politics or any controversial issue, or take part in political activity, must inform their line manager in advance; the manager should consult Chief Adviser Politics if there is a risk to impartiality or perception of impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone intending to seek nomination as a party candidate or declare independent candidacy must notify their line manager, who should consult Chief Adviser Politics before public declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on the BBC must be impartial and avoid 'we'
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with issues concerning the BBC itself, reporting must remain duly impartial, accurate and fair; there should be clear editorial separation between those reporting and those presenting corporate positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenters and reporters should avoid conflicts of interest and it is normally inappropriate to refer to the BBC as 'we' or the content as 'ours'. Personal experience can be included if appropriate and signposted, without compromising impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include contentious views but challenge and offer alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of expression means including views some audiences may find offensive; contributors expressing contentious views must be challenged while being given a fair chance to respond and alternative perspectives should normally be offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should acknowledge possible offence and be robust, fair and dispassionate. Minority views should be given appropriate space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory referral where serious offence or impartiality risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If content may cause serious offence but failure to reflect it could affect impartiality, or if there's a risk either of causing serious offence or jeopardising impartiality, referral must be made to a senior editorial figure who should consult Editorial Policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Sections on Harm and Offence for detailed triggers and thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of contributors' affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume contributors are unbiased. For contributors from charities, think-tanks, universities, or individuals, it may be necessary to give appropriate information about affiliations, funding or particular viewpoints where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key test: would the audience be misled if such information was not available? Consider whether affiliations risk undermining trust in contributor's credentials or authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and labelling of supplied news material
rubrics_metrics.description: Video/audio news releases or material supplied by outside organisations may be used only when the BBC cannot gather it and its use is justified by editorial significance; such use may jeopardise impartiality if offered as a way to avoid scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extracts should be clearly labelled, stating who supplied them and explaining relevant circumstances of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider editorial risks of technology and AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of technologies such as automation or artificial intelligence may impact perception or reality of impartiality; content makers should consider editorial risks and legal/rights/data protection/security issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A senior editorial figure must oversee deployment and continuing use of any AI and should seek advice from Editorial Policy, who may consult the AI Risk Advisory Group before deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI in commissioning and distribution needs oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: For independent productions, any proposed use of AI with material impact on audience-facing content should be discussed in commissioning. Products that use AI to distribute or curate content are editorial experiences and are subject to editorial approval and human oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A senior editorial figure must be responsible for compliance within the production team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to audiences but avoid over-weighting responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Listening and engaging with audiences and including their perspectives is central, but responses should not be given wider significance than they merit and care must be taken not to misrepresent weight of opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate scrutiny to audience opinions and ensure debate does not discount audience members who support a minority view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering protests and demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Protests and demonstrations are routine news; interviews should be impartial, rigorous and challenging and include alternative perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess risk that previewing might encourage participation; withdraw if a peaceful protest becomes violent and presence inflames situation; take particular care when using material posted by protesters on social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny and questioning consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: BBC journalism should scrutinise arguments, question consensus and hold power to account with consistency and due impartiality; levels of scrutiny should be based on degree of power, responsibility and accountability of the contributor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate scrutiny to government, bodies holding power, opposition parties, campaigners, experts, academics and sometimes members of the public; source and attribute alternative or contradictory information where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns, initiatives and social action — independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where BBC content highlights issues others campaign on, it should not endorse those campaigns or allow itself to be used to campaign to change public policy; BBC must remain independent and distanced from government initiatives, campaigners, charities and their agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care needed when scheduling content that coincides with third-party campaigns; advice available from Editorial Policy. Social action output must not simply embrace another group's agenda and must retain arm's-length position from government initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social action — operational constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Social action output can be part of public service but the BBC must set its own social action agenda and priorities; output must not involve on-air fundraising except for BBC charitable appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure objective treatment of groups, avoid favouring one above another, and keep news reporting of BBC social action campaigns duly impartial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case studies and cumulative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When using sympathetic case studies or individual-perspective approaches on public policy issues, consider whether such an approach may jeopardise perceptions of impartiality (eg if the individual has affiliations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inclusion of wider context or different perspectives within the item or over time; assess cumulative effect across the same service or across different services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling apparent consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues that appear to have broad or unanimous consensus may still pose risks to impartiality; the BBC should report where consensus lies and give it due weight but avoid using language or tone that accepts consensus as self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge assumptions and avoid reinforcing generalisations lacking evidence; give issues appropriate rigour and seek advice from Editorial Policy where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections and referendums — heightened scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: During election and referendum campaigns the BBC's commitment to due impartiality is closely scrutinised; special considerations apply during periods when content is being consumed by those about to vote and sometimes in the run-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific advice is available from Chief Adviser Politics, who will publish separate guidelines for each campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality in series and over time
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'series of programmes' may be considered as a whole: multiple linked pieces on same or related issues within an appropriate period aimed at a like audience should achieve due impartiality across the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan in advance, signpost intention to achieve impartiality across a series, and ensure linked programmes/items include appropriate links. Long-running output may achieve impartiality over time through consistent editorial judgement but editors must ensure a broad range of individuals and views are reflected and given due weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory referral for exceptional singular view content
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptionally, an individual programme or content not part of a series may include a singular view on a controversial subject; any such proposal must be referred to Chief Adviser Politics to ensure it meets requirements of due impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies even for personal view documentaries or drama; see related guidance on signposting and linked output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicians and political content in non-political output
rubrics_metrics.description: Inviting politicians to take part in output which would not normally include politicians, political opinions or controversial issues requires consultation with Chief Adviser Politics in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any offer from a politician to take part must be referred before acceptance or decline. Advice also available from Editorial Policy for others known for partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama, entertainment and culture — creative freedom with oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences expect artists and entertainers freedom to explore subjects from a particular perspective and the BBC is committed to offering such content; commissioners should consider range of perspectives over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commissioning drama, entertainment or cultural output covering current public policy or controversial subjects, consult Editorial Policy in advance; potential conflicts of interest may need consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal view content — transparency and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal view content (expressing highly partial views) must have its nature made clear to audiences in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such content covers controversial subjects it should maintain factual accuracy, fairly represent opposing viewpoints when included, and provide opportunity for response or alternative perspectives when appropriate. BBC staff and regular presenters associated with news/public-policy output are normally not appropriate to present such personal view content.
